text: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
a time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what is planted;
a time to kill and a time to heal; a time to tear down and a time to build;
a time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance;
a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them; a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek and a time to lose; a time to keep and a time to throw away;
a time to tear and a time to mend; a time to be silent and a time to speak;
a time to love and a time to hate; a time for war and a time for peace.
What does the worker gain from all his toil?
I have seen the task God has given to the children of man to keep them occupied.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet no one can grasp what God has done from beginning to end.
I know there is nothing better for people than to rejoice and do good while they live.
Also, that everyone should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his toil—this is the gift of God.

versions.text: And that everyone should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his toil—this is the gift of God.
versions.explanation: Beginning with "And that" leaves the sentence sounding grammatically incomplete when read aloud. "Also," renders the Hebrew וְגַם naturally and gives the verse a clean opening for oral reading.

text: I know that everything God does will endure forever; nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. God has done it so that people will stand in awe before him.
Whatever is has already been, and what will be has been before; and God seeks out what has been driven away.
And I saw something else under the sun: in the place of judgment—wickedness was there; in the place of justice—wickedness was there.
I said in my heart, "God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every deed."
I said in my heart concerning the children of man: God tests them to show them that they are but animals.
For the fate of man and the fate of the animal are one and the same: as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the animal, for everything is vanity.

versions.text: For the fate of man and the fate of the animal is one and the same: as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the animal, for everything is vanity.
versions.explanation: The compound subject ("the fate of man and the fate of the animal") requires the plural verb "are."

versions.text: For the fate of man and the fate of the animal are one and the same: as one dies, so dies the other.
versions.explanation: The final third of the verse was dropped: וְרוּחַ אֶחָד לַכֹּל ("and one breath belongs to all"), וּמוֹתַר הָאָדָם מִן־הַבְּהֵמָה אָיִן ("and man has no advantage over the animal"), and כִּי הַכֹּל הָבֶל ("for everything is vanity"). These clauses carry the argument of the passage and are restored from the earlier version, keeping the intentional grammar fix ("are one and the same").

text: All go to one place. All came from the dust, and to the dust all return.
Who knows whether the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal goes down into the earth?
So I saw that there is nothing better than for a person to rejoice in his work, for that is his portion. Who can bring him to see what will come after him?
